skeleton:
Chraime Spiced Fish

Libyan · Easy · Serves 4

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
Chraime is the Rosh Hashanah fish of the Libyan Sephardic table — fillets simmered in a fierce, sweet-sour red sauce of tomato, garlic, caraway, and cayenne, served at the New Year for the blessing of abundance and eaten at room temperature, the flavors steeping through the holiday's long table. The sauce is the argument: the fish's gentleness against the chraime's fire, and the two-day steep that makes the second day's fish better than the first's.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

Ingredients

  • the chraime's honest measure
  • the chraime's signature
- **Salt the fish 30 minutes and rinse — the firming's mercy.** The salting draws the fish's surface moisture and firms the flesh for the simmer's gentleness; the rinse lifts the salt's excess. The fish joins the sauce already-seasoned and structurally braver. - **The bridge:** the chraime's fire is the house's dial — the cayenne's honest tablespoon is the festival register, the paprika's half runs the family table, and both are true. The caraway is the chraime's own signature and not bridged: the seed's anise-mustard depth is the sauce's identity.

Chraime Spiced Fish

Prep: 25 minutes, plus 30 minutes salting · Cook: 25 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 25 minutes · Serves 4

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 800 g firm white fish fillets (grouper, sea bass, or snapper), cut to serving pieces — or 600 g mackerel, the traditional's oily strength
  • 1 tbsp salt for the 30-minute salting, then rinsed and dried
  • 4 tbsp olive oil (about 50 g); 3 onions (about 450 g), sliced thin
  • 8 cloves garlic (about 30 g), sliced — the chraime's honest measure
  • 2 tbsp tomato paste (about 30 g); 500 g tomatoes, grated, or 1 can crushed
  • 1 tbsp caraway seeds (about 8 g), lightly crushed — the chraime's signature
  • 2 tsp cayenne or sweet paprika mixed to the house's fire (about 5 g); 1 tsp cumin
  • 2 tbsp white or red wine vinegar (about 30 ml); 1 tbsp honey or sugar (about 15 g)
  • 1 tsp salt; 100 ml water (about 100 g)
  • The finish: lemon wedges, a fist of cilantro (about 15 g), and bread for the sauce's sopping

Instructions

  1. **The sauce's long build (20 minutes).** Soften the onions in the oil 8 minutes to a golden silk; the garlic and the caraway 2 minutes more; the tomato paste darkened 1 minute; the tomatoes, the cayenne, the cumin, the vinegar, the honey, the salt, and the water — simmered 10 minutes to a thick, brick-red sauce, the sweet-sour-fire balance tasted at the end. Checkpoint — the sauce's taste: fiery first, the vinegar's sour behind, the honey's sweetness rounding — and the caraway's distinctive thread through all three. It should read one notch fiercer than the serving's target (the fish's flesh and the steep will calm it).
  2. **The fish's gentle simmer (8–10 minutes).** The salted, dried fish pieces slid into the barely-simmering sauce, spooned over, covered, and poached at the tremble (barely 90 °C) 8 to 10 minutes — until the flesh just turns opaque at its thickest and the flakes part at the nudge. Checkpoint — the fish's law: the pull at the thickest piece's flake — just-opaque, holding its shape, the oil's slick at the surface's edge. A boiled chraime is a broken fish, and the 10-minute ceiling is the whole clock's mercy.
  3. **The steep and the room-temperature service.** The pot cooled, then refrigerated — served at the room's temperature (the Rosh Hashanah truth) or gently rewarmed, the cilantro and lemon at the table, the bread for the sauce. Checkpoint — eating test: the fish's firm-sweet flesh carrying the sauce's full argument — the fire, the sour, the sweet, the caraway's thread — steeped through the overnight's rest (the second day's fish is the dish's own finest, the flavors run deep). The bread sops the sauce's red to the last. It should taste like the New Year's own blessing: abundance's fish, the fire's celebration, and the patience that carries both.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Fish broke at the simmerBoiled, or the salting skippedThe 30-minute salt; the 90 °c poach
Sauce one-note fierceThe vinegar-honey balance un-runThe sweet-sour's equal spoons, tasted
Caraway's thread absentSeeds whole, un-crushedThe light crush releases the depth

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- The chraime's own law: made ahead, steeped 1 to 2 days, and better for it — keeps 3 days refrigerated. The sauce's batch keeps a week for the next fish. - Variations: the mackerel's oily strength (the festival's own), the shrimp's quick cousin. The #37 fish tagine is the chermoula register's seat; this record is the fire-and-caraway's.
